title: Tokio Marine cools on Suncorp
full_text:
Tokio Marine is understood to have cooled on its Suncorp takeover ambitions temporarily after a share price rally in the $21.6bn Brisbane-based insurance firm.
Shares in Suncorp have gained 7 per cent in the past month and 24 per cent in the past six months, which sources say puts the business out of Tokio Marine’s price reach for now.
However, should circumstances change, such as a major weather event causing shares to fall, it would probably move swiftly to bid for the target.
Comparisons can be drawn with Challenger, where major Japanese shareholder Dai-ichi moved on Australia’s largest annuity provider after its share price fell by $1 since August.
The Japanese suitor advised by Bank of America is expected to have its $11.80-a-share offer that values the company at $8bn rejected by Challenger’s board, but it is expected to return with a higher offer.
Goldman Sachs and Jarden are advising Challenger.
DataRoom understands that Suncorp has held preliminary discussions with Tokio Marine in recent months, with executives travelling to Japan, despite not receiving an approach.
The insurance firm told the market last month that it had not received an offer and that there were no discussions regarding a takeover.
Tokio Marine is one of the largest insurance firms globally. It has reinsurance deals with both Suncorp and IAG.
An insurance industry expert said Australia was an attractive market: it was largely a duopoly consisting of IAG and Suncorp.
Sources said if a deal were to happen, it would come towards the end of Suncorp CEO Steve Johnston’s tenure. He was appointed to the top job in 2019.
Suncorp’s defence adviser is JPMorgan, while Goldman Sachs was busy on an insurance deal, which led some to believe it was working with Tokio Marine.
DataRoom first reported in July that Tokio Marine was undertaking work on potential acquisition targets in Australia.
It sent representatives to Australia in August to carry out further exploratory work for a potential $20bn-plus purchase of one of the nation’s top insurance firms.
It is understood that the Japanese financial group had executives on the ground, meeting with representatives of Insurance Australia Group and Suncorp, along with other industry experts in what was understood to be detailed analysis of the two potential targets and the sector.
Tokio Marine wants to embark on a transaction to put excess capital to work, and analysts say it told the market about five months ago it wanted to break into the Australian or Canadian markets with a major acquisition.
Founded in 1879, Tokio Marine operates in more than 50 countries and regions and has more than 50,000 employees.
Insurers globally are reaping a windfall from inflation-fuelled price increases, justified partly by the threat of catastrophic events brought on by climate change.
As a result, they have recorded near-record profits and prospered on the back of higher interest rates, as their cash holdings generate more earnings. Suncorp shares closed down 3c at $20.39 on Friday.
